blogs.title: Deference at the Doorstep of Transparency: How Farahi Reinforces Agency Authority Under Exemption 7(A)
blogs.description: This post examines the D.C. Circuit’s reliance on longstanding deference doctrines when evaluating FBI assertions that records were compiled for law‑enforcement purposes. It traces precedent from Campbell v. DOJ through Clemente v. FBI, analyzes why national‑security investigations receive heightened deference, and discusses the implications for congressional oversight and future FOIA challenges against intelligence agencies.

blogs.title: "From Ongoing to Stale": Decoding the ‘Pending or Reasonably Anticipated’ Test After Farahi
blogs.description: Focusing on the temporal element of Exemption 7(A), this article unpacks how the court assessed whether enforcement proceedings remained pending or reasonably anticipated despite years elapsing since the original investigation began. It reviews CREW’s vagueness concern, Juarez’s guidance on ongoing investigations, and offers a framework for litigants to demonstrate either continuation or cessation of proceedings in similar cases.

blogs.title: When Redaction Isn’t Enough: The Segregability Hurdle in Massive FBI Files
blogs.description: This piece delves into the statutory requirement that agencies make reasonable efforts to segregate non‑exempt material before withholding whole documents. Using Farahi’s 10,750 pages and 80 CDs as a case study, it explores how courts determine ‘reasonable segregation’ versus ‘inextricably intertwined’ material, surveys prior decisions such as Mead Data Center and Perioperative Services, and considers whether emerging data‑segmentation technologies could reshape agency compliance.

blogs.title: Closed‑Door Evidence: The Growing Role of Ex Parte Declarations in FOIA Battles
blogs.description: Analyzing the use of sealed ex parte filings in Farahi, this article evaluates how courts treat confidential declarations when adjudicating exemption claims. It discusses procedural fairness concerns raised by plaintiffs who cannot see the underlying evidence, reviews prior rulings like Perioperative Services & Logistics LLC v. VA, and proposes reforms—such as mandatory public summary statements or protective‑order protocols—to balance secrecy needs with litigants’ due‑process rights.
